sections.h2: Where is the Columbus County Register of Deeds, and when does it take documents?
sections.html:
The Columbus County Register of Deeds sits at 125 Washington Street, Suite B in Whiteville, with a mailing address of PO Box 1086, Whiteville, NC 28472. The office is open from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, except county holidays.

Plan to arrive early on closing day. The office states that it takes no documents for recording after 4:45 p.m. on any day, even though the doors stay open until 5:00. Marriage license applications close even earlier, at 4:30 p.m.

Anyone selling a home in Columbus County will deal with this office at the end of the process, because the deed that moves title and the deed of trust that secures a buyer's loan are both recorded here. A seller does not normally walk the paper over in person. The closing attorney or title office usually handles that step, but knowing the cutoff helps you read a closing calendar.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Columbus County?
sections.html:
A standard deed costs $26.00 to record for the first 15 pages, plus $4.00 for each page after that. The county's fee notice cites G.S. 161-10, which sets the same uniform schedule for every North Carolina register of deeds.

Recording fees printed on the Columbus County Register of Deeds fee schedule
DocumentFee as printed
Deed of trust$64.00 for the first 35 pages, then $4.00 per added page
Other instruments (deeds, easements, most agreements)$26.00 for the first 15 pages, then $4.00 per added page
Plat$21.00 per page
UCC filing$38.00 for 2 pages, $45.00 for 3 to 10 pages, plus $2.00 per page past 10
Satisfaction or cancellation of a deed of trustNo fee
Certified copy of a document$5.00 first page, $2.00 each added page
Assignment that references more than one original instrument$10.00 for each added reference
  • The release of a paid-off mortgage costs the seller nothing to record.
  • Plain copies made at the counter or requested by mail run 25 cents a page, and deeds on the office's online system can be viewed at no charge.
  • A notary oath taken at the office carries a $10 fee payable by cash or local check.

sections.h2: How does the excise tax on a Columbus County deed work?
sections.html:
The seller pays it, and the register collects it before the deed is recorded. State law sets the rate at $1.00 for each $500.00 of the price or value conveyed, counting any fraction of $500 as a full unit (G.S. 105-228.30). The Columbus County office describes the same rate on its FAQ page as $2 per thousand dollars of the purchase price.

Half the money stays with the county general fund and half goes to the Department of Revenue. Because the amount is tied to the sale price, the closing statement will show it as a line item, and you can ask the closing attorney for the figure before you sign.

The register's staff cannot tell you the tax on a given sale without the deed in hand. A deed that only changes the names on title still needs a new deed drawn up and recorded, at the same $26.00 first-15-pages fee. The office advises seeing an attorney for the drafting, and notes that excise tax may also apply.

sections.h2: Can I record or search Columbus County land records online?
sections.html:
Yes. The county accepts electronic recording of every document type except plats, and a list of approved vendors is on the e-recording page of the register's website. Electronic filing lets a closing package reach the office before the 4:45 p.m. cutoff without anyone driving to Whiteville.

The online index is name based. The office says plainly that its retrieval system cannot tell you who owns a particular street address, so a search starts with a seller or buyer name rather than a house number. For parcel-by-parcel ownership by address, use the county tax office, which keeps the land records and mapping staff.

  • Search by owner name on the register's public system and open the recorded deed.
  • Compare the legal description on that deed with your tax bill.
  • Check the deed of trust section for any mortgage with no matching satisfaction.
  • Ask the Clerk of Court, not the register, about mechanics liens and judgments. The register's FAQ points those questions to the courthouse.

sections.h2: Why does the recording date matter to a Columbus County seller?
sections.html:
It sets who wins if two claims compete for the same land. Under G.S. 47-18, a conveyance, option, lease of more than three years, or right of first refusal does not bind lien creditors or buyers who paid value until it is registered in the county where the land lies, and priority follows the order of registration.

That rule is why a signed deed alone does not finish a sale. Until the Columbus County register stamps it with a recording time, a later claim could still jump ahead.

The same logic applies to owner financing. Chapter 47H covers a contract for deed with five or more payments on a one to four family home when the seller keeps title. The seller must record the contract, or a memorandum of it, within five business days, and the buyer can cancel until midnight of the third business day. If you are weighing that route in a county where many homes are modest, read the whole chapter before signing.

sections.h2: What farmland notice appears on Columbus County land records?
sections.html:
Columbus County posts a notice under Session Law 2018-113 that land records must alert title researchers when a tract sits within one-half mile of a poultry, swine or dairy qualifying farm, within 600 feet of any other qualifying farm, or within one-half mile of a voluntary agricultural district.

For a seller, that means a buyer's title search may flag the proximity. The statute adds that no cause of action arises from a researcher's failure to report it, and that licensed brokers and appraisers are not liable for omitting it. It is a notice, not a restriction on the sale. In a county with 938.12 square miles of land and about 54 people per square mile (Census Bureau, 2020), farm neighbors are common, so expect the question and answer it early.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about selling a house in Columbus County?
sections.html:
Columbus County is a small, rural market with lower prices than most of the state. The Census Bureau estimates 50,487 residents for July 2025, down from 58,098 in the 2010 census, and counts 23,724 housing units.

  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $146,000 (2020-2024).
  • Owner-occupied housing unit rate: 71.1%.
  • Median household income: $49,442 in 2024 dollars.
  • Median gross rent: $824 a month.
  • Residents 65 and older: 22.2%.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 55.

With 55 permits in 2025 and a population below its 2010 level, new construction is thin. Price your expectations against the $146,000 median, and ask your closing attorney which county records to pull before you list.

sections.h2: How do property taxes fit into a Columbus County sale?
sections.html:
County tax bills are due September 1 and can be paid by mail, phone, online, drop box or in person at the Columbus County Tax Office, which uses PO Box 1468 in Whiteville. The office lists online payment through columbus.webtaxpay.com.

State law lets a bill be paid at face value until January 6. After that, interest of 2% applies from January 6 to February 1, then three-fourths of one percent for each month or fraction after (G.S. 105-360). The lien for real property tax attaches as of the date property is listed under G.S. 105-285 (G.S. 105-355), so the seller's bill follows the parcel into the sale.

Ask the tax office for a payoff figure before closing, and give it to whoever prepares the settlement statement. Senior exemptions are handled by the same office. State relief for owners 65 or older or disabled uses Form AV-9 filed with the county assessor, so ask the tax office for the current paperwork.

faqs.q: Who records the deed when I sell a house in Columbus County?
faqs.a: The Columbus County Register of Deeds in Whiteville records it. Your closing attorney or title office normally submits the deed, either in person or through an approved electronic vendor, and the office stops accepting documents at 4:45 p.m.

faqs.q: What is the recording fee for a deed in Columbus County?
faqs.a: It is $26.00 for the first 15 pages and $4.00 for each added page, per the county fee schedule and G.S. 161-10. A deed of trust costs $64.00 for the first 35 pages.

faqs.q: Does the seller or the buyer pay the deed excise tax in Columbus County?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The register collects it before recording, at $1.00 for each $500.00 of price or value, and the county FAQ describes this as $2 per thousand dollars.

faqs.q: Can the Register of Deeds look up who owns a certain address?
faqs.a: No. The office says its retrieval system is name based, so a search needs a person or company name. Use the county tax office for address-based parcel records.

faqs.q: Where do I ask about liens and judgments on a Columbus County property?
faqs.a: Ask the Clerk of Court at the courthouse. The Register of Deeds FAQ sends mechanics lien and judgment questions there, and also check recorded deeds of trust for any unreleased mortgage.
